section_summary: This section comprises U.S. consular despatches from Taihoku and Manila, internal State Department memoranda, cross-reference sheets, and an extensive voluntary report detailing political developments and Japanese colonial administration in Taiwan between 1936 and 1940. It covers the uncovering and judicial prosecution of the 1934 'Shuyu Kai' anti-Japanese revolutionary plot, as well as analyses of Formosa's strategic role as an economic and military base for Japan's southward expansion into South China and Southeast Asia. The primary focus of the section is Vice Consul John K. Emmerson's exhaustive study of 'Kominka' (the Japanization movement), which details the aggressive wartime assimilation campaign to remodel the culture, language, political structures, and religious practices of the Formosan Chinese and indigenous aborigines into loyal imperial subjects.

subfiles.about: Transmits press translations regarding the discovery, background, and judicial sentencing of members of the anti-Japanese revolutionary secret society Shuyu Kai.
subfiles.from: Edward B. Maney, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.summary: American Consul Edward B. Maney reports on the lifting of a two-year press ban concerning an alleged Formosan Chinese conspiracy to incite revolt, overthrow the Government-General, and restore Taiwan to China. The plot was organized by Sai Shuku Kai and fortune-teller Bo So So under the cover of the religious secret society 'Shuyu Kai' and local 'Parents Societies' (Fubo Kai). Enclosed translations from the Taiwan Nichi Nichi Shimpo describe the background and socio-economic profile of the 425 arrested suspects and report on the guilty verdicts and prison terms handed down to ten defendants at the Tainan Local Court.
subfiles.title: Suppression of Alleged Formosan Revolt Plot (Shuyu Kai Incident)
subfiles.to: Erle R. Dickover, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Forwards an article summarizing Formosa's role as a springboard for Japanese political, military, and economic expansion in South China and the South Seas.
subfiles.from: Henry B. Day, American Vice Consul, Manila
subfiles.summary: American Vice Consul Henry B. Day transmits a copy and summary of Chen Han-seng's article 'Formosa as Base of Japanese Expansion' from The Commonwealth Advocate. The report details Japan's ten-year development program emphasizing strategic infrastructure, military airfields, and harbor development to project influence southward. It also discusses subsidized Japanese and Formosan emigration to Fujian and Guangdong, extraterritorial protections exploited by Formosans in Amoy, mining ventures in Guangxi, and extensive smuggling operations into Swatow.
subfiles.title: 'Formosa as Base of Japanese Expansion' by Chen Han-seng

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 894a.20/12 regarding general conditions in Taiwan and local developments reflecting the China conflict.
subfiles.summary: This Document File Note serves as a cross-reference entry for Despatch No. 894a.20/12 (recorded under 894A.00/24), dated August 27, 1937, from Consular Officer Rowe in Taihoku. The underlying document reports on general conditions in Taiwan and recent developments reflecting the outbreak of hostilities in China.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: General Conditions in Taiwan (Despatch No. 894a.20/12)

subfiles.about: Reports on political developments, military inspections, and wartime mobilization in Taiwan connected with the China Incident, enclosing the gubernatorial conference agenda.
subfiles.summary: Consul Gerald Warner surveys political and wartime developments in Taiwan, including Prince Higashikuni's ten-day air inspection tour, the arrival of a forty-ship naval fleet at Keelung, and the convening of the Governors Conference by Governor-General Kobayashi. The report notes the dispatch of 1,000 young Formosan farmers in the Farm Volunteer Corps to cultivate land near Shanghai and comments on the failure of residents in the Pescadores to purchase patriotic bonds. An enclosed translation details the agenda for the Governors Conference, covering national spiritual mobilization, air defense preparations, commodity controls, and aborigine training.
subfiles.title: Political Developments in Taiwan Connected with the China Incident
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Tokyo Despatch No. 3039 enclosing an intelligence report on the strategic importance of the port of Takao.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This Document File Note cross-references Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 3039 (filed under 794.00/131, recorded under 894A.00/26), dated June 22, 1938, from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. The referenced despatch analyzes the significance of the port of Takao in relation to Japan's 'Southward Advance' policy and encloses an intelligence report transmitted to the Italian Admiralty by the Italian Naval Attaché in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Port of Takao and Japan's 'Southward Advance' Policy (Despatch No. 3039)

subfiles.about: Brief routing memorandum calling the Secretary of State's attention to the summary tags of the report on the Japanization of Taiwan.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.summary: Adviser on Political Relations Stanley K. Hornbeck submits a brief routing memorandum to Secretary of State Cordell Hull. Hornbeck advises that the summary tags covering Vice Consul Emmerson's report on the 'Japanization of the People of Taiwan' are well worth noting.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on the 'Japanization of the People of Taiwan' Report

subfiles.about: Recommends an official performance grade of 'Excellent' for Vice Consul Emmerson's voluntary report on 'Kominka'.
subfiles.from: Cabot Coville, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Cabot Coville of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs reviews Taihoku's voluntary report of December 2, 1939, entitled ''Kominka' or the Japanization of the People of Taiwan'. FE recommends a rating of 'Excellent' for this thorough, well-documented, and useful study. Coville notes that Vice Consul John K. Emmerson has since returned to his assignment in Osaka.
subfiles.title: Evaluation of Vice Consul Emmerson's Report on 'Kominka'
subfiles.to: DAA and DCA, Department of State

subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan's colonial assimilation policy in Taiwan and highlights the disparity between Japanese imperial rhetoric and practical domination.
subfiles.from: Cabot Coville, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Cabot Coville submits an analytical memorandum to Stanley K. Hornbeck and Secretary of State Cordell Hull reviewing Vice Consul Emmerson's findings. The memorandum points out that Japanese administrative policy in Taiwan is structured for the distinct advantage of Japanese nationals at the expense of the subjugated Chinese population. Coville concludes that the Taiwanese experience contradicts Japanese propaganda concerning an egalitarian 'new order' in East Asia, as Japanese superiority and dominance are deeply resented by the Formosan populace.
subfiles.title: Analysis of Japan's Colonial Assimilation Policy in Taiwan
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and Cordell Hull, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Summarizes the key findings and factual data of Vice Consul Emmerson's report on the Japanization of Taiwan for Far Eastern Affairs leadership.
subfiles.from: Cabot Coville, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Cabot Coville provides an extensive four-page summary of Vice Consul Emmerson's report for Joseph W. Ballantine and Maxwell M. Hamilton. The memorandum reviews the Japanese dominance over local assemblies, quasi-compulsory neighborhood organizations (chokai and hoko), and the aggressive campaign enforcing Japanese language fluency through police registries. It further notes educational discrimination, compulsory labor mobilizations, Shinto religious replacement, aborigine administration, and the ironic surge of interest among Formosans in learning Mandarin Chinese.
subfiles.title: Detailed Summary of Report on 'Kominka' or Japanization of Taiwan
subfiles.to: Joseph W. Ballantine and Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Examines Japan's extensive administrative, educational, social, and religious campaign to transform the people of Taiwan into loyal Japanese imperial subjects.
subfiles.from: John K. Emmerson, American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.summary: Vice Consul John K. Emmerson presents an in-depth study of the 'Kominka' movement in Taiwan, intensified after the outbreak of the China Incident. The report examines official and unofficial organs of political control—such as local assemblies, urban chokai, and the traditional rural hoko system—which are utilized for surveillance, labor mobilizations, and anti-British agitation. It investigates language dissemination, educational segregation, the prohibition of traditional Chinese customs, the state promotion of Shinto over Chinese temples, and the experimental establishment of a model Japanized county and village in Chureki. The text in this section concludes with an examination of the legal, educational, and police administration of Taiwan's indigenous aborigines.
subfiles.title: 'Kominka' or the Japanization of the People of Taiwan
